# Key Issues and Developments in U.S. Immigration Enforcement

## Mass Deportation Campaign and ICE Operations

The Trump administration has pursued an aggressive mass deportation agenda, with a stated goal of removing 1 million immigrants in the current year [29]. ICE has conducted sweeping enforcement operations in cities including Chicago, Los Angeles, Minneapolis, and others, with agents conducting raids at farms, construction sites, apartments, grocery stores, and even schools [19]. The administration's budget for ICE grew by $75 billion under the "One Big Beautiful Bill," dramatically expanding the agency's resources and surveillance capabilities [19].

## Disputed Tactics and Civilian Deaths

One of the most contentious developments has been the killing of U.S. citizens during enforcement operations. The deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis — both American citizens killed by federal agents — triggered widespread protests and became a central flashpoint in congressional funding negotiations [14][29]. An off-duty ICE agent also killed Keith Porter in Los Angeles [14]. These incidents prompted Democrats to refuse further DHS funding without substantive reforms to ICE operations [3][29].

## Deployment to Airports During DHS Shutdown

A partial Department of Homeland Security shutdown — stemming from a congressional dispute over immigration enforcement funding — halted routine DHS funding in mid-February, leaving TSA workers without pay for over six weeks [29]. As a result:

- More than 3,200 TSA workers (about 11% of the workforce) missed work on a single day, and at least 458 quit altogether [16][29]
- Over 40% of Atlanta airport's TSA agents called out on some days [8]
- In Houston, security lines stretched across three floors with wait times exceeding four hours [20]

In response, the Trump administration deployed ICE agents to 14 major airports — a move described as **"unprecedented in the 100-year history"** of Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport by Mayor Andre Dickens [8]. Former acting ICE Director John Sandweg noted that using ICE agents near TSA checkpoints "has never happened in the history of the agency" [24]. Critics, including TSA union leaders, argued ICE agents lacked the specialized training to meaningfully reduce lines and called the move a political distraction from the real issue: unpaid TSA workers [16][24].

## American Citizens and Children Caught in the Dragnet

ProPublica and congressional investigators documented that more than 170 U.S. citizens had been detained by immigration agents, including over 20 children [6]. Specific cases include:

- A family with an 11-year-old recovering from brain cancer who was deported despite having hospital documentation [6]
- A 16-year-old U.S. citizen, Arnoldo Bazan, who was tackled and placed in a choke hold by agents chasing his undocumented father [6]
- A Canadian mother and her 7-year-old autistic daughter detained at a Texas checkpoint, with the child struggling with stress and overstimulation at the Dilley Detention Center [10]

A Senate/House minority staff report compiled 128 cases of children — citizens and non-citizens — who were "injured, left unattended or otherwise put at risk" by DHS enforcement operations [6].

## Fear and Disruption in Immigrant Communities

Immigrant families have been living in acute fear, with many effectively housebound. One undocumented family in Chicago stopped going out entirely, with their son experiencing sleepwalking episodes shouting "Get down! They're gonna see us!" [19]. ICE has deployed extensive digital surveillance, including license plate readers, facial recognition technology, and Palantir's ELITE system to track individuals [19]. Long Island farms and vineyards have also been severely impacted, with the Farm Bureau estimating that up to 65% of the agricultural workforce consists of seasonal migrants [12].

## Congressional Deadlock and Proposed Reforms

Senators from both parties raced to broker a deal to end the DHS shutdown, with the emerging proposal seeking to:

- Fund most of DHS, but **exclude ICE's enforcement and removal operations**
- Require body cameras for ICE officers
- Potentially mandate judicial warrants (rather than administrative warrants) for home searches [3][29]

Democrats demanded stronger reforms, including unmasking of agents and bans on enforcement at sensitive locations like schools and churches [29]. The shutdown negotiations were further complicated when President Trump linked DHS funding to passage of the SAVE America Act, a voter ID bill, before eventually backing off that demand [3][29]. Newly confirmed DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin replaced the ousted Kristi Noem amid public backlash over enforcement methods [26][29].

## Legal Challenges

At the Supreme Court, justices appeared sympathetic to the Trump administration's defense of the "metering" policy — which allows border officials to turn away asylum seekers when ports of entry are deemed overburdened — with a ruling expected by end of June [7]. The administration has also successfully obtained emergency Supreme Court rulings allowing deportation of migrants to third countries and revocation of temporary legal status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans [7].

## Broader Social and Political Fallout

The enforcement crackdown has galvanized significant public opposition. "No Kings" protests have drawn millions nationwide, with religious leaders across faiths citing immigration enforcement as a core moral concern [2]. A union representing 32,000 Southern California hospitality workers warned employers that housing ICE agents constituted "unusually dangerous conditions," particularly ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup [14]. At the same time, high-profile crimes committed by individuals who entered the country illegally — such as the alleged murder of Loyola University student Sheridan Gorman by a Venezuelan national who had been released under Biden-era catch-and-release policies — have been cited by the administration to justify the crackdown [5][15].
